Content:
Recall that
[MATH: \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}]
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = {\color{blue}\artanh{x}} + C, \qquad {\color{blue}x\in(-1,1)}.]

Content:
But we have just seen that

Content:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = {\color{red}\arcoth{x}} + C, \qquad {\color{red}x\in(-\infty,-1) \cup (1,\infty)}.]

Content:
Notice that the integral on the left-hand side is the same but we used different functions on the right. What is the difference, and how do we know which hyperbolic function to use?

Content:
The difference is the domain of the variable [MATH: x.] When the [MATH: |x| < 1,] we use the antiderivative [MATH: \artanh{x},] otherwise we use the antiderivative [MATH: \arcoth{x}.]

Content:
For instance, we have that

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{− 1/2}^{1/2}(1)/(1 − x^{2})dx|= artanh x|_{− 1/2}^{1/2}; = artanh ((1)/(2)) − artanh (− (1)/(2)).]

Content:
Note that since the limits of integration lie in the interval [MATH: (-1,1),] we used the antiderivative [MATH: \artanh{x}.]

Content:
While, on the other hand, we have that

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{2}^{3}(1)/(1 − x^{2})dx|= arcoth x|_{2}^{3}; = arcoth (3) − arcoth (2).]

Content:
Note that since the limits of integration lie in the interval [MATH: (1,\infty),] we used the antiderivative [MATH: \arcoth{x}.]
